title: Formal Verification: Bridging Proofs and Testing

questions.prompt: Which statement expresses the fundamental insight of the lecture about testing and formal verification?
options: Testing shows the presence of bugs; formal verification proves their absence
Testing proves the absence of bugs; formal verification shows their presence
Testing and formal verification both prove the absence of all possible bugs
Testing finds design flaws; formal verification finds only coding errors
Testing proves correctness; formal verification estimates how often bugs occur
questions.explanation: Testing runs a finite set of inputs, so it can reveal bugs but not rule them out, while formal verification constructs a mathematical proof that they are absent. The reversed statement swaps the two roles.

questions.prompt: Exhaustively testing a 64-bit processor requires 2^64 (about 18 quintillion) test cases. At 1 billion tests per second, approximately how long does the lecture say this would take?
options: About 635 years
About 18 years
About 64 years
About 6,350 years
About 2,048 years
questions.explanation: The state space explosion example states that 2^64 test cases at 1 billion tests per second would take approximately 635 years, which is why exhaustive testing is infeasible.

questions.prompt: In the argument for why testing isn't enough, what does the "needle in a haystack" problem refer to?
options: Critical bugs lurk in rare combinations of concurrent events and timing conditions
The number of test cases grows exponentially with the size of the input
Static analysis tools report many bugs that turn out not to be real
Proof assistants need a human to guide every step of a proof
Properties must be written in temporal logic before they can be checked
questions.explanation: The needle-in-a-haystack problem is about rarity: critical bugs hide in rare combinations of concurrent events, fault scenarios and timing conditions, and at millions of requests per second such "extremely rare" events happen regularly. Exponential growth of test cases is the separate state space explosion problem.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts testing and formal verification?
options: Testing covers only the tested cases; formal verification covers all possible inputs and states
Testing covers all possible inputs and states; formal verification covers only the proven cases
Testing covers design and implementation; formal verification focuses only on the implementation
Testing constructs a mathematical proof; formal verification runs a finite set of inputs
Testing can prove the absence of bugs; formal verification can only prove their presence
questions.explanation: Testing runs a finite set of inputs, so its coverage is the tested cases only, while formal verification constructs a proof covering ALL possible inputs and states. It is formal verification, not testing, whose scope covers both design and implementation.

questions.prompt: On the formal methods spectrum of rigor, which pairing of technique and computational complexity is correct?
options: Model checking: PSPACE-complete
Static analysis: undecidable
Theorem proving: polynomial
SMT solving: PSPACE-complete
Model checking: NP-complete
questions.explanation: The spectrum lists static analysis as polynomial, model checking as PSPACE-complete and theorem proving as undecidable, with SMT solving (NP-complete) as the enabling technology. NP-complete belongs to SMT solving, not model checking.

questions.prompt: In model checking, how are the system and the properties to be checked expressed?
options: System as a finite-state machine; properties in temporal logic
System in temporal logic; properties as a finite-state machine
System as source code; properties as unit test assertions
System as random inputs; properties as minimal counterexamples
System in formal logic; properties as a correctness certificate
questions.explanation: Model checking takes a system model (a finite-state machine) and properties written in temporal logic; the tool then explores all reachable states and returns either a proof or a counterexample.

questions.prompt: In LTL, □ means "always", ◇ means "eventually", → means "implies" and ¬ means "not". Which formula states "Every request eventually gets a response"?
options: □(request → ◇response)
◇(request → □response)
□(response → ◇request)
□(¬request → ◇response)
◇(request → ◇response)
questions.explanation: □ applied to (request → ◇response) says that at every point, a request implies that a response eventually follows. Starting the formula with ◇ instead would require this at only some single point, not for every request.

questions.prompt: In theorem proving, what role does the machine (the proof assistant) play?
options: It verifies every step of a proof that a human guides
It automatically explores every reachable state of the model
It generates random inputs and shrinks any failing case
It approximates program behavior without running the code
It finds the whole proof automatically with no human input
questions.explanation: Theorem proving is interactive: a human guides the proof construction and the machine acts as a meticulous assistant that verifies each step, producing a correctness certificate. Automatically exploring all reachable states describes model checking.

questions.prompt: Which strength does theorem proving offer that distinguishes it from model checking?
options: It can handle infinite state spaces
It is fully automated from end to end
It requires little expertise to use
It always runs in polynomial time
It produces concrete counterexamples
questions.explanation: Theorem proving handles infinite state spaces and offers the strongest guarantees, while model checking suffers from state space explosion in large systems. Full automation and concrete counterexamples are model checking's strengths, whereas theorem proving is labor-intensive and needs significant expertise.

questions.prompt: Which static analysis technique is described as safely approximating program behavior?
options: Abstract interpretation
Symbolic execution
Data flow analysis
Type systems
Bounded checking
questions.explanation: Abstract interpretation safely approximates program behavior. Symbolic execution runs the program with symbolic instead of concrete values, data flow analysis tracks how data moves through programs, and type systems catch errors at compile time.

questions.prompt: A team wants a fully automated technique that finds bugs without running the code and scales to a very large codebase. They can accept occasional reports of bugs that aren't real. Which approach fits best?
options: Static analysis
Theorem proving
Model checking
Property-based testing
Exhaustive testing
questions.explanation: Static analysis finds bugs without running code, is automated and scales to very large codebases, at the cost of possible false positives (reporting bugs that aren't real). Model checking is also automated but is limited by system scale.

questions.prompt: A team needs deep, foundational verification and is willing to build proofs interactively with a proof assistant. Which tool from the verification toolbox fits?
options: Coq
TLA+
Alloy
SPIN
Z3
questions.explanation: Coq (INRIA, France) is the proof assistant for deep, foundational verification. TLA+ and SPIN are model checkers, Alloy does bounded checking for software design, and Z3 is an SMT solver used as a backend for many tools.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Amazon's use of TLA+ is correct?
options: A 939-line DynamoDB spec found 3 bugs, one with a 35-step trace
An 804-line S3 spec found 3 bugs, one with a 35-step trace
A 102-line EBS spec found only 2 subtle bugs in the service
Amazon reports that engineers need 1-2 months to learn TLA+
A 939-line DynamoDB spec found no bugs, confirming its design
questions.explanation: The 939-line DynamoDB spec found 3 bugs, including one with a 35-step trace that would be "nearly impossible" to find via testing. The 804-line S3 spec found 2 bugs, the 102-line EBS spec found 3, and Amazon says engineers learn TLA+ in 2-3 weeks.

questions.prompt: A developer tests a buggy reverse function with the property `for any list x, reverse(reverse(x)) == x`. After generating random inputs, the framework finds one that fails. What does a property-based testing framework do next?
options: Shrinks it to the smallest input that still reproduces the bug
Explores all reachable states to prove that the failure is real
Reports it as a false positive and keeps generating new inputs
Issues a correctness certificate covering all the passing inputs
Rewrites the property as a temporal logic formula and rechecks it
questions.explanation: Property-based testing defines a property, generates hundreds or thousands of random inputs, and on failure shrinks to a minimal counterexample: the smallest possible input that reproduces the bug.

questions.prompt: The Intel Pentium FDIV bug (1994) occurred in roughly 1 in 9 billion random divisions and led to a $475 million recall. What was the underlying flaw?
options: 5 missing entries in a 2,048-cell lookup table of the division unit
A 64-bit float converted to a 16-bit signed integer, causing overflow
Software reused from an older chip without being re-verified for it
A deadlock between concurrent floating-point division operations
A rounding error in 1 of every 2,048 floating-point divisions
questions.explanation: The floating-point division unit returned incorrect results because 5 entries were missing from a 2,048-cell lookup table. The 64-bit-to-16-bit conversion overflow is the Ariane 5 bug, not the Pentium bug.

questions.prompt: What was the bug behind the Ariane 5 Flight 501 explosion (1996)?
options: A 64-bit float for velocity overflowed when converted to a 16-bit signed integer
A 16-bit signed integer for velocity lost precision when converted to a 64-bit float
Five missing entries in a lookup table produced wrong floating-point divisions
A deadlock between two guidance processes stopped all velocity updates
A 32-bit altitude value overflowed when converted to an 8-bit unsigned integer
questions.explanation: A 64-bit float representing velocity was converted to a 16-bit signed integer; the value was larger than 32,767 and overflowed, leading to a software exception, guidance system failure and self-destruct. Missing lookup-table entries describe the Pentium FDIV bug.

questions.prompt: What lesson does the lecture draw from the Ariane 5 Flight 501 failure?
options: Reused software must be re-verified; static analysis could have detected the bug
Software that worked on Ariane 4 could safely be reused without further checks
The bug could only have been found by flight testing the real rocket
The bug was detectable only by theorem proving, not by static analysis
Floating-point hardware must be checked against lookup tables before launch
questions.explanation: The software was reused from the slower Ariane 4 without re-verifying it for Ariane 5's faster trajectory, so the lesson is that reuse requires re-verification. Post-accident analysis showed the bug was detectable by static analysis.

questions.prompt: Which statement about industries where formal methods are standard practice is correct?
options: DO-178C, via its DO-333 supplement, allows formal methods as an alternative to testing for avionics
ISO 26262, via its DO-333 supplement, allows formal methods as an alternative to testing for avionics
NASA uses the Coq proof assistant as its standard theorem prover for aerospace work
DO-178C is the automotive functional safety standard for brake control and steering
Hardware design adopted formal methods as standard practice because of the Ariane 5 explosion
questions.explanation: In aerospace, DO-178C (via the DO-333 supplement) allows formal methods as an alternative to testing for avionics, and NASA uses the PVS theorem prover. ISO 26262 is the automotive standard, and hardware design has used formal methods since the Pentium bug.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture's key insights, how do testing and formal verification fit into a mature engineering process?
options: Both are necessary parts of the process, since they serve different goals
Formal verification replaces testing once a proof of correctness exists
Testing alone is sufficient as long as enough random inputs are generated
Formal verification is too costly to use outside academic research projects
Property-based testing fully replaces both unit testing and formal verification
questions.explanation: Under the "tale of two goals" insight, testing finds bugs while verification proves correctness, and both are necessary parts of a mature engineering process. Formal methods are also used daily at Amazon, Microsoft, Intel and NASA, so they are not limited to research.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to start applying formal thinking right away with the smallest learning investment. Which option from the recommended learning path fits, with its approximate learning time?
options: Property-based testing with Hypothesis for Python, about 1 day
Design modeling with Alloy, about 1 day
TLA+ for distributed systems, about 1 week
Deep verification with Coq via Software Foundations, about 2-3 weeks
Property-based testing with Hypothesis for Python, about 1-2 months
questions.explanation: The learning path recommends property-based testing (Hypothesis for Python) to start now, with about 1 day of learning. Alloy design modeling takes about 1 week, TLA+ about 2-3 weeks and Coq via Software Foundations about 1-2 months.
